title: Size-aware shard dispatcher + priority prefetch to cut embedding p99 for short requests
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem: We continue to see high tail latency on the embedding endpoint that disproportionately affects short requests (<=64 tokens). Large or long-lived requests can monopolize kernel execution and inflate queueing for small, latency-sensitive requests. Existing coalescing and microbatch heuristics reduce average cost but leave p99 for small requests at unacceptable levels for customer-facing features (semantic search, instant rerank).

Proposal: Implement a size-aware shard dispatcher combined with a short-request fast-path and priority prefetching. Key ideas: (1) classify incoming requests by token-length buckets and route small requests to a light-weight shard pool that favors low-inflight and short scheduling windows, (2) add a priority queue layer that gives the fast-path shard preemptive enqueue tokens and jittered prefetch so short requests can fold into warm kernels without stalling long jobs, (3) emit kernel prewarm hints after observing hot short-request patterns, allowing pre-compilation and warmed KV cache on shards dedicated to fast-paths, (4) soft preemption: allow preemptible long-running batches to yield to high-priority short requests with bounded cost and rollback safety.

We intentionally avoid wholesale changes to microbatching logic; instead this is an orthogonal routing & scheduling layer that reduces head-of-line blocking and improves p99 for latency-sensitive requests while keeping throughput and unit-cost regressions small.
acceptance_criteria: p99 latency for requests <= 64 tokens drops to < 120ms in the canary region compared to baseline p99 (baseline ~260ms)
end-to-end median latency for small requests does not regress by more than 10%
throughput (tokens/sec) for mixed workloads regresses by < 5% at 95% confidence in internal perf runs
no embedding quality regression (cosine similarity distributions within statistical margin on existing benchmark prompts)
feature flags and rollout gating exist to revert shard routing without client impact
QA and canary dashboards surface per-shard p50/p90/p99, queue depth, kernel-warm hits, and preemption counts
implementation_plan: Design: finalize shard classification thresholds and soft-preempt semantics (1 week)
Runtime: implement size-aware dispatcher and priority queue layer; add APIs for prewarm hints (2 weeks)
Kernel: add light-weight kernel prewarm path on fast-path shards and safe preemption checkpoints (1 week)
Control plane: feature-flag per-customer and per-region routing; metrics and tracing hooks (3 days)
Integration: end-to-end tests + canary in eu-west-1 then us-west-2 (5 days)
Rollout: staged traffic ramp + monitor + rollback plan (3 days)
testing_plan: Unit tests for dispatcher classification and priority queue correctness
Integration tests that simulate mixed short/long workloads and validate preemption invariants
Performance benchmarks against representative traffic replay (mix derived from production logs) to measure p50/p90/p99 and throughput
A/B canary in a single region with traffic shards reserved for fast-path; compare telemetry vs control
Quality checks: run existing embedding regression suite (semantic search + rerank prompts) to ensure no vector drift
rollout_plan: Deploy behind feature flag to staging and run synthetic replay for 24h
Canary: enable in eu-west-1 for 5% of traffic for 48h, monitor p99, queue depth, kernel errors
Ramp to 25% for 24h if metrics stable, then to 50% for 24h
Full global ramp if no regressions, with automated rollback on p99 or error spikes beyond thresholds
Post-rollout: 7-day retention of extra observability metrics (per-shard heatmaps)
progress_updates: 2025-02-19: Spike completed. Verified that classifying by token count and routing to separate queues reduces simulated head-of-line blocking in the replay harness.

2025-02-24: Prototype dispatcher implemented. Found a trade-off: very small shards (<4 GPUs) can experience throughput cliffs when saturated. Decided to use dynamic shard sizing tied to observed short-request qps.
2025-02-27: Kernel prewarm hint API landed (PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4821). Prewarm lowers cold-kernel misses for fast-path by ~65% in synthetic tests.
2025-03-03: Integration tests show p99 reduction of ~52% on replay data in staging when fast-path shards have warm kernels; throughput impact measured at -3.7% for mixed workload.
2025-03-05: Beginning canary deployment in eu-west-1 under feature flag. Monitoring dashboards configured at dashboards/redwood/emb-shard-latency
notes: Risk: If short-request shard sizing is misconfigured, small requests may experience queuing during sudden traffic spikes; mitigation is autoscaling + conservative initial shard size
Potential follow-ups: integrate request-level QoS tokens that are billable, explore priority-aware batching within fast-path shard
We will coordinate with SRE on alert thresholds for preemption counts and kernel rollback events
